cards.explanation: The answer is money. The text says the Pharisees were "…lovers of money…" Jesus had just said that no servant can serve two masters, God and money (Luke 16:13). Hearing that and scoffing anyway tells you where their hearts were.
The answer is scoffing, friends. The text says they "…were scoffing at Jesus." They heard the whole teaching, and the text tells us they scoffed. Scoffing at a talk you just heard is a bold move.

The answer is detestable. Jesus says, "For what is prized among men is detestable before God." That's strong language, and it comes right after He says God knows their hearts. So people can be impressed by something while God sees it differently. That's why I check the oven and not just the compliments.

The answer is the gospel of the kingdom of God. Jesus says, "Since that time, the gospel of the kingdom of God is being preached…" The gospel is the good news. The Law and the Prophets were proclaimed until John, and the kingdom of God is now what's being preached. That's a big change in the message, friends.

The answer is a single stroke of a pen. Jesus says, "…it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for a single stroke of a pen to drop out of the Law." That's about the smallest mark you could make. Even that tiny mark won't drop out of the Law.

The answer is False. Jesus says, "…he who marries a divorced woman commits adultery." He says it right after talking about the man who divorces his wife and marries another woman. It's a serious teaching, and He speaks plainly here.

The answer is the crumbs from the rich man's table. The text says Lazarus was "…longing to be fed with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table." I deal with crumbs every day in my bakery, and I sweep them up without a thought. I think this one hurts, because for Lazarus those crumbs were what he longed for.

The answer is True. The text says, "Even the dogs came and licked his sores." It's a rough detail, and I think it's there to show how hard Lazarus had it. This part is heavy, friends, and I won't pretend it isn't.
The answer is to Abraham's side. Abraham was Israel's forefather (Luke 1:73). The text says Lazarus "…was carried by the angels to Abraham’s side." Carried, friends, not walking, and not on his own.

The answer is Lazarus cooling his tongue with water. The rich man says, "Father Abraham, have mercy on me and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue." The ask is small, just the tip of a finger. This part of the story is heavy, and I think we should let it be heavy.

The answer is comforted. Abraham says, "But now he is comforted here, while you are in agony." Lazarus is the beggar who lay at the gate with sores. The word for him now is comforted, and that's a big turn from the gate.

The answer is cross. Abraham says the chasm is there "…so that even those who wish cannot cross from here to you, nor can anyone cross from there to us." Notice the rich man can see Abraham and call out, and Abraham answers him. Seeing and calling were never the problem, friends. The chasm blocks crossing.
The answer is True. The rich man says, "…for I have five brothers." He's still thinking of his family, friends. I think it shows his mind has turned toward the ones he left behind.

The answer is to warn them. The rich man says, "Let him warn them, so that they will not also end up in this place of torment." He's asking for his five brothers, friends. He wants them warned so they don't end up where he is.

The answer is the Prophets. Abraham says, "They have Moses and the Prophets; let your brothers listen to them." So the brothers already have something to listen to. That's Abraham's answer to the request to send Lazarus.

The answer is False. Abraham says, "If they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead." The rich man had said they would repent if someone came from the dead, and Abraham doesn't agree. This is a serious word, and it's the last one in the story.
